summary: Defines a binary format for representing HTTP messages. It gives a way to write requests and responses as bytes outside of a live HTTP connection. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Web messages are usually plain text on the wire. This is a compact packed form for the same messages so they can be saved or passed along easily.

questions: how to encode http messages in binary form
how does binary http encode requests and responses
known length vs indeterminate length http messages
subtitle: A compact byte format for writing down an HTTP request or response outside of a live HTTP connection.

tldr.problem: HTTP messages normally exist only inside a protocol exchange, in the text form of HTTP/1.1 or the framing of HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. There is no simple, standalone way to store or transform a whole message, for example to encrypt it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9292 defines a binary format in which a message is a framing indicator, control data, a header section, content and a trailer section, with every length and number written as a variable-length integer. It comes in a known-length form and an indeterminate-length form.
tldr.outcome: The format gets the media type message/bhttp. It carries HTTP semantics but not every wire detail, so it is not meant for exact recording of how a message was encoded.

today: RFC 9292 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2022. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to its metadata.

sections.title: Why a Binary HTTP Message Format
sections.content:
RFC 9292 defines a simple format for representing an HTTP request or response so that it can be conveyed outside an HTTP protocol. That makes it possible to transform an entire message, including applying authenticated encryption to it.

The design is informed by the framing of HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, and the rules for building messages rely on HTTP/2, but the format itself is distinct. It is a binary alternative to the message/http content type defined for HTTP/1.1. The RFC says a binary format permits more efficient encoding and processing, and also reduces exposure to security problems related to processing of HTTP messages.

The format is designed to convey the semantics of valid HTTP messages as simply and efficiently as possible. It is not designed to capture every detail of how a specific HTTP version encodes a message, so it is unlikely to suit applications that need an exact recording.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally a web message only exists while two computers are talking. This gives the message a neat packed shape so you can keep it, lock it up or hand it on.

sections.title: What a Binary Message Contains
sections.content:
A binary message is built from the same parts that HTTP messages always have, written out as a sequence of bytes. In order, they are:

  • a framing indicator, a single integer that says whether this is a request or a response and how the rest is laid out;
  • for a response, zero or more informational responses, each with a status code and a header section;
  • control data: the method and target for a request, or the status code for a response;
  • a header section with zero or more header fields;
  • content, which is zero or more bytes;
  • a trailer section with zero or more trailer fields;
  • optional padding of zero-valued bytes.

All lengths and numeric values use the variable-length integer encoding from QUIC (RFC 9000). Integers do not have to be written in the fewest bytes possible.
sections.plainLanguage: A message is like a packing list: a label saying what kind of message it is, then the address, then the notes, then the parcel itself, then any last notes.

sections.title: Known-Length and Indeterminate-Length Forms
sections.content:
The RFC describes two ways to encode a message. In the known-length form, the header section, the content and the trailer section each start with a length prefix that counts the bytes that follow, not including the length field itself. Because of the variable-length integer encoding, each field section and the content can be at most 2^62-1 bytes.

In the indeterminate-length form, used when lengths are not known when encoding starts, only the content has length prefixes. Content is sent as any number of chunks, each with a non-zero Chunk Length, followed by a zero Content Terminator. A field section is a series of field lines ended by a zero Content Terminator. That zero is unambiguous because a field's Name Length cannot be 0.

The framing indicator tells a reader which form it has and whether the message is a request or a response. Any other value makes the message invalid.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes you know how big the parcel is before you pack it, so you write the size on the box. Sometimes you are still packing, so you pack in pieces and put a stop sign at the end.

sections.title: Control Data, Status Codes and Field Lines
sections.content:
Request control data is an ordered sequence of four length-prefixed values: Method, Scheme, Authority and Path. They follow the rules of the :method, :scheme, :authority and :path pseudo-header fields in HTTP/2. Where HTTP/2 might omit :authority, this format encodes a zero-length value instead.

Response control data is just the status code, encoded as a variable-length integer rather than a decimal string. Informational responses use codes from 100 to 199. They are written by repeating the control data and header section until a final status code from 200 to 599 appears.

A field line is a length-prefixed name (at least one byte) and a length-prefixed value. A message is invalid if it contains fields named :method, :scheme, :authority, :path or :status. Connection-related fields cannot have their usual effect here and SHOULD be removed, though their presence does not make a message invalid. Several cookie fields are combined with a semicolon rather than a comma, as in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.
sections.plainLanguage: The control data is the address on the front of the envelope. Each note inside is written as a label and its value, one pair at a time.

sections.title: Padding, Truncation and Invalid Messages
sections.content:
A message can be padded with any number of zero-valued bytes. Non-zero padding makes the message invalid, although a processor MAY choose not to check padding bytes.

Truncation saves space when the end of a message is empty. If the trailers are empty, an encoder MAY leave them out instead of writing a zero length. It MAY leave out empty content in the same way if the trailers are also empty. A message cut off at any other point is invalid. Decoders MUST treat missing truncated fields as if their length were zero.

Invalid messages MUST NOT be processed further except to log an error and produce an error response. The format is designed for incremental processing, so an implementation has to be aware that an error might be found after it has already acted on part of the message.
sections.plainLanguage: You can add blank pages at the end for padding, and you can skip empty last pages. But if a page in the middle is torn off, the whole letter is thrown out.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC encodes a simple GET /hello.txt request with four header fields in both forms. The known-length encoding begins with framing indicator 0 and the indeterminate-length encoding with framing indicator 2. The request example notes that the Host header field is not copied into the authority value, as is required to reproduce the request accurately. In the known-length example the last two bytes, covering content and trailers, can be removed without changing the meaning. The indeterminate-length example carries 10 bytes of padding, so up to 12 bytes could be removed.

A response example includes informational responses with status codes 102 and 103 followed by a 200 response. The RFC points out that the reason phrase text is not kept by this encoding. A chunked HTTP/1.1 response can be encoded in the indeterminate-length form to minimize buffering, but chunk boundaries and chunk extensions are not retained.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples take an ordinary web request and show it packed down into a few lines of numbers, once with sizes written first and once with stop signs.

sections.title: Differences from HTTP Protocol Messages and the Media Type
sections.content:
Because it is a standalone representation, this format lacks several features of the interactive protocol versions. The RFC lists chunk extensions and transfer encoding, generic framing and extensibility, multiple field blocks other than one header and one trailer block, reason phrases in responses, header compression, and response framing that depends on the request (such as HEAD) or the status code (such as 204 or 304). Unlike HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, it uses a fixed layout for control data rather than pseudo-fields.

CONNECT and upgrade requests can be represented, but the RFC says doing so serves no purpose, because they exist to change protocol behavior and this format cannot do that without extra mechanisms.

IANA has added the media type message/bhttp, which can hold a single HTTP request or response provided it obeys the MIME restrictions for message types. Only the 8bit or binary encodings are permitted.
sections.plainLanguage: The packed form keeps what a message means but leaves out some extras that only matter while two computers are mid-conversation.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Most of the security issues that apply to handling HTTP messages apply here too. The RFC says that strict parsing with no tolerance for errors can help avoid a number of attacks.

Implementations still need to guard against resource exhaustion from large messages, especially messages with many fields. The format is designed to need minimal state, but building a combined field value may commit resources. The RFC singles out the cookie field when a message is translated for another context, such as an API or HTTP/1.1, where the recipient may not expect multiple values.
sections.plainLanguage: Be strict when you unpack the message, and do not let someone swamp you with a giant box full of tiny notes.

data.title: Known-Length Request
data.code:
Known-Length Request {
  Framing Indicator (i) = 0,
  Request Control Data (..),
  Known-Length Field Section (..),
  Known-Length Content (..),
  Known-Length Field Section (..),
  Padding (..),
}
